blocks.text: When Wetzstein [=Johann Gottfried Wetzstein, notes communicated to Löw, cited in Aramäische Pflanzennamen] (Pf. [=Löw, Aramäische Pflanzennamen] 420) objects that the fruit of the terebinth is not edible, this is inaccurate, for Oken [=Lorenz Oken, Allgemeine Naturgeschichte für alle Stände (Botanik)] 1755 reports that the terebinth kernel is eaten in the Levant and therefore comes to market. The seeds are also eaten in Greece (see above 192).

Before the true pistachio was introduced into Eretz Yisrael, the native terebinth kernel will have been more highly valued and could very well be mentioned among the export articles of early times. The Septuagint and the Vulgate therefore quite correctly understand boṭnīm as terebinth kernels.

Furrer [=Konrad Furrer, articles in Schenkel's Bibel-Lexikon] (Bibellexikon sv. [=sub voce]) tries to get around the difficulty that the pistachio grows in Syria but not in Eretz Yisrael with the turn of phrase that the pistachio is “nowadays” rarely found in Eretz Yisrael any more, whereas it “once probably” occurred there “more frequently”. This is incorrect. The tree did not grow in Eretz Yisrael in antiquity either, and for remote antiquity pistachios could at most come into consideration as transit goods, if one wished to assume, against the sources, that the tree already grew in Syria in high antiquity.

Antiquity regarded the pistachio as a hybrid of the almond tree and the terebinth, which contains a recollection of its late appearance: jKil. [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Kilayim (ed. Krotoschin)] 1, 27^{a}_{52} לוזים ובוטמין (not, as Aruch [=Aruch (Nathan b. Yeḥiel), ed. Kohut] u. a. [=and others], בוטנין); Ḳazwīnī [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] 2, 25: حبّة الخضراء [ḥabbat al-khaḍrāʾ] grafted onto لوز [lawz] yields fustuḳ. Thus according to the jer. [=Jerusalem (Palestinian)] Talmud, Pf. 69, according to the gr. [=Greek] Geoponica writers and Kaleb [=Aderet Elijahu, Goslow 1835, appendix by Kaleb Afendopulo] 17^{a}.
Hebr. [=Hebrew] boṭnīm belongs to aram. [=Aramaic] buṭma, has the same meaning, and was treated under P. [=Post, Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai] Terebinthus (s. [=see] above 192).

In Mishnaic Hebrew the pistachio is called פסתקין pl. [=plural], derived from pers. [=Persian] pišteh (ZDMG. [=Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft] 50, 646), like syr. [=Syriac] ܦܣܬܩܐ [פסתקא]*) [Samar. [=Samaritan (Targum)] ביצטקין Gn. [=Genesis] 43, 11 LA. [=variant reading] ביסטקין], and borrowed from this arab. [=Arabic] fustuḳ**).

ܦܣܛܩܐ [פסטקא] Gal.-Üb. [=Syriac translation of Galen] 293 (read with t instead of ṭ), ܦܣܬܩܐ [פסתקא] (= Jacob v. [=of] Edessa, Leyden, Nöld.-OS. [=Orientalische Studien Theodor Nöldeke gewidmet] 575) List [=Gottheil, A list of plants] 208, ܦܣܬܩܐ [פסתקא] Geop. [=Lagarde, Geoponicon in sermonem syriacum versorum] 75_{25}. This is Honeins [=Ḥunain ibn Isḥāq]'s correct spelling, BB. [=Bar Bahlūl, Lexicon syriacum] 1556. It is an error when Isidorus [=Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae] derives pistakia from the fact quod cortex pomi eius nardi pistici odorem referat (Tschirch [=Tschirch, Handbuch der Pharmakognosie], Entstehung der Pflanzen- und Drogennamen 494).

Arab. [=Arabic] also in a transferred sense فستق الصنوبر [fustuq al-ṣanawbar] pine, türk. [=Turkish] فستك [fstk] Sha [=Steinschneider, Heilmittelnamen der Araber] 1465 f. [=and the following page] (Handjéri [=Handjéri, Dictionnaire français-arabe-persan et turc] sv. pistache). On hell-fustuḳ s. Flora [=Löw, Die Flora der Juden] 2, 124. fustuḳ in Arabic physicians, z. B. [=for example] Kroner, Maimūnī [=Hermann Kroner, edition of Maimonides' medical work] passim (Mb. [=?] 17. 30, 32). Pistachio resin: ʿilk al-anbāṭ E. Wiedem. [=Wiedemann, Beiträge zur Geschichte der Naturwissenschaften] 49, 19 from Nuwairī [=an-Nuwairī, Nihāyat al-arab]. Migrated further as alfocigo, alfostigo, alfonsigo (Engelmann, Gloss. [=Engelmann and Dozy, Glossaire des mots espagnols et portugais dérivés de l'arabe] 34).
